subject: zoology_2
question_text: What is crisscross inheritance? Explain the inheritance of one sex linked recessive character in human beings.

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book p.23, LAQ 8. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Revised 2026-09-05 after the examiner audit: the margin note now counts the three statements the step actually prints, and the insider note says what a complete answer contains instead of claiming a words-only answer loses marks.

steps.label: What it is
steps.why: A father passes his only X to his daughters, never to his sons, so his X-linked character can only reach a grandson through a daughter.
common_mistakes: Saying the character passes from father to son. It cannot.
steps.memory_tip: Father to daughter to grandson: the path crosses twice.
lines: T.H. Morgan observed sex linked inheritance
in Drosophila melanogaster.
An X-linked recessive character present in
a man is inherited by his grandson through
his daughter. This is crisscross
inheritance.
The two best examples are colour blindness
and haemophilia.

steps.label: Why males are more affected
steps.why: A man has only one X, so a single recessive allele on it has no partner to mask it and shows at once.
common_mistakes: Saying the gene is stronger in males. The reason is that they have only one X.
Leaving out why females are less affected.
steps.memory_tip: One X means nothing to hide behind.
steps.margin_note: Three statements cover this mark: the male's single X, why he is more prone, why the female is less prone.
lines: Males have only one X chromosome, with no
partner to mask it.
So every gene on that X, dominant or
recessive, is expressed phenotypically.
Females have two X chromosomes, so there is
more than a 50% chance of carrying a
dominant gene. They are less prone.

steps.label: What colour blindness is
steps.why: The gene for the cone pigment sits on the X chromosome, which is why the defect is inherited with sex.
common_mistakes: Placing the gene on an autosome. Red-green colour blindness is X-linked.
Blaming the rods. The cones give colour vision.
steps.memory_tip: Cones give colour; the faulty gene rides on the X.
steps.margin_note: Three short facts before the crosses.
lines: The retina of the eye has rods and cones.
The cone cells are responsible for colour
vision.
A recessive gene on the X chromosome causes
red-green colour blindness.
The dominant gene gives normal colour
vision.

steps.label: Normal woman × colour blind man
steps.why: The father gives his single Xᶜᵇ to every daughter and his Y to every son, so all daughters carry it and no son does.
common_mistakes: Giving the sons the defect in this cross. They get the father's Y.
Saying the daughters are colour blind. They are carriers.
steps.memory_tip: All daughters carry it, all sons escape it.
steps.margin_note: Write the karyotype for every person named.
lines: A woman with normal vision (AAXᶜXᶜ)
marries a colour blind man (AAXᶜᵇY).
All the daughters will be carriers with
normal vision (AAXᶜXᶜᵇ).
All the sons have normal vision (AAXᶜY).

steps.label: Carrier daughter × normal man
steps.why: The carrier mother passes either of her two X chromosomes, so half her sons receive the faulty one.
common_mistakes: Giving all the sons the defect. Half of them get it.
Missing that the grandfather's character has now reappeared.
steps.memory_tip: Half the sons affected, half the daughters carriers.
steps.margin_note: Point out the grandson. That is the crisscross.
lines: When the carrier daughter marries a man
with normal colour vision, 50% of the sons
get colour blindness.
All the others have normal vision, and 50%
of the daughters are carriers.
The colour blind character of the
grandfather has reached the grandson
through the carrier daughter.

steps.label: Both parents colour blind
steps.why: If neither parent has a normal allele to give, no child can receive one.
common_mistakes: Expecting some normal children. There are none.
Treating the daughters differently from the sons here.
steps.memory_tip: No normal gene in either parent means no normal child.
lines: When both parents are colour blind, all
their children will be colour blind.

steps.label: Colour blind mother
steps.why: A son takes his only X from his mother, so a colour blind mother passes the defect to every son.
common_mistakes: Giving the sons a chance of escaping. They cannot: their only X is hers.
Making the daughters colour blind. They get a normal X from the father.
steps.memory_tip: A son's only X comes from his mother.
steps.margin_note: Two more cases, one line each.
lines: When the mother is colour blind and the
father has normal vision, all their sons
inherit colour blindness from the mother.
All the daughters will be carriers, because
they get a dominant gene from the father
and a recessive gene from the mother.
When the mother is a carrier and the father
is colour blind, 50% of daughters and 50%
of sons get colour blindness.

steps.label: The rule that follows
steps.why: Stating the rule at the end shows the examiner that the crosses were understood and not just copied.
steps.memory_tip: Daughters take the father's X; sons take the mother's.
steps.margin_note: One boxed line closes the essay.
lines: So the X-linked characters are inherited by
daughters from their father, and by sons
from their mother.

lines.text: This is why it is called crisscross inheritance

insider_note: Write the karyotype for every person in every cross — AAXᶜXᶜ, AAXᶜᵇY and so on. The complete answer shows the genotypes of both parents and of the children in each cross, not the outcome in words alone.
